scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Xuc was created in 1942 by Francisco 'Paquito' Palaviccini in Cojutepeque, Cuscatlán.
Palaviccini sought to create a unique Salvadoran rhythm after finding no existing records of national genres during his international travels.
He based the rhythm on his observations of a musical group in Tacuba that used the juco, a friction drum.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Xuc is a celebratory dance associated with Salvadoran national pride and local harvests.
It was specifically composed for the 'fiestas de la caña' (sugar cane festivals).
It represents the 'alegría' (joy) of the Salvadoran people and is the signature rhythm of the San Miguel Carnival, one of the largest festivals in Central America.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is dynamic and characterized by small jumps and specific foot placements.
The primary step involves a 'heel-toe-heel' sequence with both the right and left feet.
Dancers also perform a crossing step where feet are kept stretched and moved back and forth while taking short jumps.
Watch for Talón-punta-talón, The Wheel.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers form wheels (circles) and move collectively while flirting.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The genre is named after the 'juco' or 'juque' instrument, which produces a 'xuc, xuc' sound.
Traditional ensembles described by Palaviccini included the teponahuaste (log drum), quijada de burro (donkey jawbone), juco, and a unique instrument made from a folded leaf placed on the tongue.
Listen for the Juco (friction drum), Teponahuaste, Quijada de burro (donkey jawbone), Tamborón.
The pulse is 2/4 or 6/8.
A bright, driving orchestral folk sound characterized by a rhythmic pulse that mimics the 'xuc-xuc' scratching of a friction drum, often featuring prominent brass and traditional percussion.

Women wear long, colorful skirts made of traditional fabric, which are essential to the choreography.
Men wear trousers made of cotton or ixtle (agave fiber).

scenes.title: The people
narration: Francisco 'Paquito' Palaviccini is the creator and primary popularizer of the genre.
Morena Celarie is the namesake of the dance group that developed the first choreography.
While born in Cojutepeque (Cuscatlán), the dance is heavily associated with San Miguel due to its carnival.
Xuc is a 20th-century creation that synthesized rural indigenous and mestizo instrumental sounds (like the juco and teponahuaste) into a popular orchestral folk genre.
